title: Why Every Python File Has That Weird __main__ Line
description:
That guard clause at the bottom of every real Python script isn't boilerplate -- it's the difference between a reusable module and a script that fires itself the moment it's imported. This Short breaks down what if __name__ == "__main__": actually checks, using the exact hello.py example from the Setup & First Program lesson. Full walkthrough -- installing Python, the REPL, and picking an editor -- is linked below.

Source lesson:
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/python-mastery-path/level-1/01-setup/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Open any real Python script and you'll spot a strange guard clause at the bottom. Here's why it's there.
This file defines a greet function, then checks a special variable before calling it. That check is the guard everyone glosses over.
Run the file directly and Python sets that variable to main, so the guard passes and greet actually runs.
But import hello.py from another script, and that same check now fails, so the print never fires automatically. That's what separates a reusable module from a script that just runs wild.

display.heading: Why it matters
display.subheading: Runs only when the file is executed directly -- not when it's imported by another module
